Transpose

tranz-POHZ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To transpose is to transfer to a different place; to switch the order of two things.

The choir director asked the pianist to transpose the hymn down a full step so more voices could reach the low notes.

Worked Example

To make the song easier to sing, the choir director transposed the entire piece up two keys before rehearsal.

Shifting something -- notes, digits, letters -- into a different position or order is exactly what transpose describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

swap: to exchange the positions of two things

invert: to reverse the position or order of

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something in its original state

maintain: to keep something unchanged

Where it sits · how much of the order changes — swap → transpose → invert

swap vs. transpose: Swap is milder than transpose: swapping seats is a quick, casual trade of two things, while transposing suggests a more deliberate, forceful switch of order inside a larger arrangement.

invert vs. transpose: Invert goes further than transpose: transposing switches two neighboring items, while inverting flips an entire order upside down, opening with what had originally been the very last scene.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — trans-

prefix — trans-: across (Latin)

root — -pose (ponere)

root — -pose (ponere): to place (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Transpose comes from Latin trans- ('across') plus ponere ('to place') -- literally 'to place across' or 'to place in a different order.' To transpose two things is to switch their places or order.

Use the root in a new word: compose
